title: On Living in Reality, Not in Anxiety
author: O. Alan Noble
summary: Noble explores the spiritual discipline of desiring good things (friendship, marriage, children, meaningful work) while not being promised their arrival. He frames this tension through the virtues of endurance, hope, and prudence, arguing that a rightly ordered desire pursued with these virtues produces stability and faith. The cultural pressure to fulfill all desires immediately pushes people toward presumption (unethical means to obtain desires) or despair (giving up entirely). Noble argues that God promises good gifts but not all earthly desires, requiring believers to act toward rightly ordered goods while remaining open to God's sovereign will and finding contentment in the bread of life God provides.
points: Rightly ordered desires (friendship, spouse, children, meaningful work) are good to pursue, but God does not promise to fulfill all of them on our timeline or in the way we expect.
Endurance (the greater part of courage) enables us to persevere through repeated rejections and failures without losing sight of the good we are pursuing.
Hope enables us to act toward rightly ordered goods without falling into presumption (sinful shortcuts) or despair (giving up), by keeping our ultimate hope fixed on Christ.
Culture pressures us to say yes to all desires immediately, creating a distorted relationship to good desires and making it nearly impossible to endure waiting for them.
Our Father's promise is not to give us everything we desire but to give us good gifts, bread for our journey, and ultimately the life abundant and the hope of resurrection.
quotes: One of the most difficult truths to internalize in this life is that you are not promised all that you desire, even when your desires are rightly ordered.
Endurance is the better part of the virtue of courage, according to Aquinas and Aristotle, for it takes more courage to endure suffering than to charge into battle.
Hope enables us to rightly pursue those desires without falling into the twin traps of presumption or despair.
Presumption is when you presume that you deserve your desire now, there's nothing to hope for, so you resort to sinful and unethical means to obtain that desire out of desperation.
Despair is when you believe there is no hope of obtaining your desire, so you stop trying, stop looking for a job or a spouse.

Our task is to ask God for good gifts. Our loving Father's promise is to give good gifts to us. He won't give us a serpent, although we all will go through difficult times in this life.” Archived from O. Alan Noble Newsletter on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
